requirement:
Each decorator on a selectable declaration is a separate `Annotation` owned
by that declaration. Stacked decorators follow the source order specified by
{cite}`requirements.sdk.outlines.attachments.order`.
rationale:
structural: No clause of `requirements.sdk.sources.typescript.attachments.decorators` prescribes how the implementation is built. The text has three parts:

- "Each decorator on a selectable declaration is a separate `Annotation`": this describes the attachment records a TypeScript or TSX outline produces. In the SDK, `Annotation` is a variant of `AttachmentKind` in `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/contents.rs`. An outline item's `attachments` list holds one record of that kind per decorator. Any implementation that returns one record per decorator, with kind `Annotation`, gives the same result. Parsing, grouping and conversion, for example in `Outline::from_legacy`, are free choices.
- "owned by that declaration": ownership means the decorator appears in the decorated item's `attachments` and not in a neighbouring item's. Callers read that list from the outline, so this is checked from the output. It does not require a particular type, ownership model or interface.
- "Stacked decorators follow the source order specified by `requirements.sdk.outlines.attachments.order`": the cited requirement says only that "Each item's attachments appear in source order". That is an ordering of output.

The requirement names no library, algorithm, signature or delegation. An implementation that emitted the same records in a different way would still satisfy it. So no implementation root needs a reference, and the empty review roots are consistent with that.

The requirement already has a `{test}` reference from `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/outline_content.rs#fn[typescript_and_tsx_decorators_belong_to_the_decorated_declaration]`. That test checks each decorator's owner, kind and span. I did not assess test adequacy.

behavioral: The marked test `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/outline_content.rs#fn[typescript_and_tsx_decorators_belong_to_the_decorated_declaration]` adequately covers the subject. It runs over both `.ts` and `.tsx` input. I read `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/languages/typescript.rs#fn[attachment_target]` only to see which decorator placements exist. I took the expected behavior from the requirement.

Obligations and the scenarios that cover them:

- **Each decorator is a separate `Annotation` owned by its declaration.**
  - The test flattens every item's `attachments`. It asserts `attachment.kind == Annotation` for each one. It compares the exact `(item.selector, source[attachment.span])` pairs.
  - Class decorators are owned by `class[Widget]`. Method decorators are owned by `class[Widget]/method[render]`.
  - Each decorator is its own record: `@sealed` and `@register("widget")` are two records on `class[Widget]`.
  - An exported default abstract class is covered. `@published(...)` sits before `export default abstract class Base`, so the decorator is a child of the export statement. It is owned by `class[Base]`.
  - A decorator nested inside another decorator's arguments (`@local class Local {}`) is owned by `class[Base]/class[Local]`, not by `Base`.
- **Only selectable declarations own decorators.**
  - The field decorator `@field value = 0;` sits directly before `render`'s decorators. The parameter decorator `@input` is on `render`'s argument. Neither appears in the exact record list.
  - So neither is wrongly attached to the following method or to the class.
- **Stacked decorators follow source order** (`requirements.sdk.outlines.attachments.order`). The exact ordered list asserts `@sealed` before `@register(...)`, and `@trace` before `@metrics.time(...)`. The multi-line decorator span is also checked exactly.

Residual risk: `export @dec class` and a non-exported abstract class with decorators are not exercised. Both go through the same `Parent` target branch that the tested `class[Widget]` uses. Ordering of several decorators on an exported declaration is not tested separately. I treat these as variants of already-covered classes, not as distinct obligations. The test's assertions would fail on any wrong owner, count or order in the scenarios it exercises, so I found no gap.
